questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: That the university I chose had not only relevant courses at my academic level in English, but also had pre-planned living spaces for their students.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was blindsided by the fact that the agreement between Copenhagen University and Nagoya University stipulated 8 credits worth of courses being equivalent to 30 ECTS, while Nagoya University insisted I take 16 of their credits to recieve my certificate of completion. I was asked by UCPH to follow Nagoya University's plan, which resulted in a very large amount of coursework (especially considering UCPH did not approve Japanese language courses as appropriate, since they were not at Master's level). I would have liked more information about the agreement in advance - perhaps a revision of the briefings about the agreement is in order.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Nagoya University had a lot of informative orientations and documents to consult for both important and niche information, including stuff like how to register for bike-parking, how to deal with culture shock, and where to purchase certain items at reasonable prices (pillows, cutlery, cooking supplies, groceries).

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Nagoya University had a lot of informative orientations and documents to consult for both important and niche information, including stuff like how to register for bike-parking, how to deal with culture shock, and where to purchase certain items at reasonable prices (pillows, cutlery, cooking supplies, groceries).

How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Nagoya University allocates housing to every international student that requests it, either in buildings on the medical campus, or near the main eastern campus. The rent and utilities are very reasonable in price, though rooms are small. Each room has an accompanying bathroom and refrigerator.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer:
There are common kitchens in each dorm building, though to different degrees. I stayed at International Residence Daiko, that had two common kitchens per floor, including storage space for cutlery, groceries and cooking implements. There are induction 'stovetops', microwaves, electric kettles and toaster ovens available for cooking. There is also a rental service for rice cookers.

Other dorms had similar equipment, though I have heard that one was in disrepair, with a common refrigerator instead of one in each room.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: You will need to purchase any and all cooking implements (pots, knives, plates, pans, mugs) for your stay, as very little cutlery and no cooking tools are provided by the dorm. They can be purchased, but the price can add up - I spent about 15000 yen on cooking implements for the semester. Your milage may vary.

Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Nagoya University dedicated a whole day to course registration, and provided spreadsheets and overviews of teachers, periods and other course information. They also provided help in the form of documentation and workshops to help complete course registration. Registration was done both online and in person, with a starting period where you were able try out courses to see whether you wanted to stick with them or not.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: A large scale orientation, workshops, fliers and documents detailing course registration.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was able to join every class that I wanted to.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: If at all possible, you should join the Japanese classes provided by the partnered institution at Nagoya University. It provides a common space for international students across schools, and a lot of friendships were created that way. Japanese may be difficult, but it is a lot of fun to learn.

questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level of difficulty varied wildly. Some introductory courses within my field had professors with an uninspiring teaching style, namely Professor -NAME REDACTED-. Others were within fields I had never before studied. Most courses provided me with a challenging but incredibly insightful look into fields of the Humanities that I had no experience with. I recommend especially Professor -NAME REDACTED- litterature courses.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: My courses at UCPH have had a common throughline in not only theme, but also teaching style. The classes at NU varied a lot, according to what professor was teaching. Some professors required a lot of reading, and focused on discussion in the classroom. Others ran the classes mostly as seminars, where participation wasn't really required (neither in the form of reading or discussion).

questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I especially enjoyed the course 'Seminar on Language and Culture in English-speaking Countries IIb' by Professor -NAME REDACTED-. It was informally called 'Comparative Culture', and was about the depiction of foreign cultures from ancient Greece to modern day. It focused on discussion, and each reading for the class was thoughtprovoking and placed within its historical context. Big thumbs up.

I also enjoyed Second Language Acquisition II a lot. It is very much a linguistics class for research students at the end of their education, but the high level of skill from each student meant it was a very inspiring class.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Though the Shinkansen rail system is very convenient, it became by far the largest contributor to unexpected costs. Each trip took about 11000 JPY (550 DKK). Having to purchase cooking supplies was also unexpected.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Fruit and greens are very expensive in Japan, as is cheese, bread and butter. Making food for yourself may be a bit more expensive than expected, if you want to eat similarly to back home.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
There are more than a hundred clubs available, so I will not list them all. They are avaiable on the NU website.
Keep in mind that many clubs/circles are all centered around being competitive (whether sports, music or something else), and people without Japanese skills will therefore have a hard time learning stuff they don't already know. The leaders of the clubs seldom have the time, ressources or English skills to instruct new members.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: There are several clubs centered around cultural exchange. All of these are good places to become friends with Japanese students and practice Japanese.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
If going to Tokyo, I especially enjoyed Shimokitazawa and Asakusa. You can find practically any hobby in Tokyo, provided you set aside the time to travel to that location (which may take longer than expected due to the chaotic subway system of Tokyo). 
Aoshima is an island in the southern part of Japan, and one of the most interesting places I have ever been. It has beautiful museums and sculptures made by a large collective of Japanese artists.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It can take a lot of time for some, but if you calm yourself, and make friends with some international students, you can adjust at your own pace.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
Join one of the cultural exchange clubs, and you will be sure to meet some Japanese students. Practice your Japanese often, they will be worse at English than you might expect.
Nagoya University has a tutoring service that is free, and gives you a Japanese student as a kind of local guide, and to help with your studies. You should take them up on that offer!

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: It was really hard to ride my bike anywhere. The cities aren't really designed for it.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The Japanese have a culture of eating out, which means restaurant prices are very reasonable. I really liked going to izakaya and karaoke with my Japanese friends as well.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Make your room feel like home! Bring stuff that makes you feel safe and reminds you that you are not alone (pictures of your family, decorations, etc.)
Try out stuff you wouldn't normally do! I had a fun time exploring activities that I had never tried - Onsen, karaoke, darts bars, jazz festivals. Take some of your international student friends with you!
Plan tourist trips in advance! It may be difficult to book hotels in certain periods in Japan, especially around Golden Week and other holidays. Make a list of the places you would like to go, and when you think you will be able to go there. The academic calendar is very similar year to year, and can be found online.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Courier services that transfer you luggage to and from the airport are very convenient, and commonly used. They cost about 3000 yen per suitcase (150 kr), but will save you a lot of trouble when you arrive jetlagged and dead tired in the blazing heat of summer.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting to know the other students, and recieving recognition for my accomplishments in my studies back home.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The amount of coursework. I had little time for tourism due to the weird communication with UCPH about how many credits I was supposed to take.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
